Through its quiet, satirical examination of a university building renovation, the story offers the reader a unique perspective on modern institutional bureaucracy and the precariousness of the humanities in contemporary academia. In particular, it provides a poignant insight into why workers sometimes endure hazardous or absurd conditions: the fear that halting work or vacating their physical space will simply prove to budget-conscious administrators that their entire department is expendable. Additionally, it highlights the often-invisible class divide in academia, showing how "work from home" mandates disproportionately affect precarious junior researchers like Noor, whose living conditions do not accommodate it.
